raw_response.printed_headline_estimate: Mann-Whitney U tests on 2000-2010 municipal-level changes (N = 320 municipalities in Minas Gerais: n = 64 served exclusively by IPO-listed state utility COPASA vs. n = 256 served exclusively by municipal organizations; 95% reliability / alpha = 0.05, PDF pp. 4-5, 9-10): (1) increase in % of households with water supplied by the general network significantly poorer under COPASA than municipal organizations (p < 0.05, Fig. 3, p. 9); (2) change in % of households connected to the general sewage or rainwater network (Fig. 5, p. 10) and % with bathrooms/WCs (Fig. 4, p. 10) non-significant at 95% reliability (p >= 0.05); (3) reduction in % of households with no bathroom/WC significantly lower under COPASA (p < 0.05, Fig. 6, p. 10). Note: Table 7 and box-plot Figs. 3-6 are raster images in the PDF, so exact numeric cells/U-statistics/p-values inside the figures/tables are not in the extracted text layer.
raw_response.publication_year_note: Published in Ambiente & Sociedade, São Paulo, v. XVIII, n. 3, p. 249-268, jul.-set. 2015 (submitted 17/08/2014; accepted 17/11/2014; DOI suffix V1832015). No conflicting online-first year printed.
raw_response.rationale: The full text empirically evaluates a narrow Criterion 2 Family C utility ownership/corporatization mechanism—management by Minas Gerais's state water and sanitation company COPASA (partially privatized via a 2006 stock-exchange IPO) versus local municipal/autonomous public service organizations—on Criterion 4 household water and sanitation access outcomes across municipalities in Minas Gerais using IBGE 2000 and 2010 Census data. Specifically, the authors compute 2000-2010 municipal first-differences for municipalities exclusively served throughout the decade by COPASA (n = 64) versus municipal organizations (n = 256, total N = 320) and apply independent-samples Mann-Whitney U tests at 95% reliability (alpha = 0.05). COPASA municipalities exhibited a significantly smaller increase in the percentage of households connected to the general water network (Fig. 3, p < 0.05) and a significantly smaller reduction in households lacking a bathroom/WC (Fig. 6, p < 0.05), while differences in 2000-2010 changes for general sewage/rainwater network connection (Fig. 5) and bathroom/WC presence (Fig. 4) were not statistically significant at the 95% level. Although Tables 2-12 and Figures 1-8 are embedded as raster images in the PDF (requiring visual inspection of the PDF pages to transcribe exact numeric medians/means or exact p-values if printed inside the plots), the prose itself provides directionally interpretable inferential two-group change contrasts, group sample sizes (64 vs. 256), and 95%-confidence significance results directly eligible for Family C SWiM synthesis.
